title: Skip the LSAT? The Rutledge Guide to Test-Free Law School Admissions: ABA and Non-ABA Law
description: Can you get into law school without the LSAT? Yes. This guide shows you how, and what each route costs you. Skip the LSAT? maps the routes into law school and the bar that don't run through an admissions test. It tells you which routes are real, who each one is open to, and what you give up by taking it. It also tells you when taking the LSAT is the better choice, and helps you work out whether that applies to you. Most people should take the LSAT. If you already know where you will live and practice, want a law degree for work you already do, or live a life that crosses borders, you may be one of the few who can skip it. Here is how to start law school sooner, and what to check before you pay a deposit. title: Constitutional Law and Precedent: International Perspectives on Case-Based Reasoning
description: This collection examines case-based reasoning in constitutional adjudication; that is, how courts decide on constitutional cases by referring to their own prior case law and the case law of other national, foreign, and international courts. Argumentation based on judicial authority is now fundamental to the resolution of constitutional disputes. At the same time, it is the most common form of reasoning used by courts. This volume shows not only the strengths and weaknesses of such argumentation, but also its serious methodological shortcomings. The book is comparative in nature, with individual chapters examining similar problems that different courts have resolved in different ways. The research covers three types of courts; namely the civil law constitutional courts of Germany, Italy, Poland, Lithuania, and Hungary; the common law supreme courts of the United States, Canada, and Australia; and the European international courts represented by the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union. The authors are distinguished scholars from various countries who specialise in constitutional justice issues. This book will be of interest to legal theorists and practitioners, and will be especially insightful for constitutional court judges. title: Law, Technology and Dispute Resolution: The Privatisation of Coercion (Law, Science and So
description: The use of new information and communication technologies both inside the courts and in private online dispute resolution services is quickly changing everyday conflict management. However, the implications of the increasingly disruptive role of technology in dispute resolution remain largely undiscussed. In this book, assistant professor of law and digitalisation Riikka Koulu examines the multifaceted phenomenon of dispute resolution technology, focusing specifically on private enforcement, which modern technology enables on an unforeseen scale. The increase in private enforcement confounds legal structures and challenges the nation-state’s monopoly on violence. And, in this respect, the author argues that the technology-driven privatisation of enforcement – from direct enforcement of e-commerce platforms to self-executing smart contracts in the blockchain – brings the ethics of law’s coercive nature out into the open. This development constitutes a new, and dangerous, grey area of conflict management, which calls for transparency and public debate on the ethical implications of dispute resolution technology.  if(window.mix_csa){window.mix_csa('[cel_widget_id="tell-amazon-desktop_DetailPage_1"]', '#CardInstance_mmdtu8V2ALXlBsaXVnZUw')('mark', 'bb')} if(window.uet){window.uet('bb','tell-amazon-desktop_DetailPage_1',{wb: 1})} ._tell-amazon-desktop_style_tell_amazon_icon_core_report__Fs1ah{color:#0f1111;color:var(--aok-sfs-color-page-primary-normal-fg,#0f1111);display:inline-block;-webkit-filter:none;filter:none;-webkit-filter:var(--aok-sfs-effect-mode-dark-color-silhouette-white,none);filter:var(--aok-sfs-effect-mode-dark-color-silhouette-white,none);height:20px;margin-right:4px;width:20px}._tell-amazon-desktop_style_tell_amazon_modal_spinner__3bz5K,._tell-amazon-desktop

title: Terrorism, Criminal Law and Politics: The Decline of the Political Offence Exception to Ex
description: Recent atrocities have ensured that terrorism and how to deal with terrorists legally and politically has been the subject of much discussion and debate on the international stage. This book presents a study of changes in the legal treatment of those perpetrating crimes of a political character over several decades. It most centrally deals with the political offence exception and how it has changed. The book looks at this change from an international perspective with a particular focus on the United States. Interdisciplinary in approach, it examines the fields of terrorism and political crime from legal, political science and criminological perspectives. title: THE COURT HAS NO JURISDICTION: Constitutional Rights vs. Municipal Codes and the Complete
description: Every day in America, millions of citizens walk into municipal courts, stand on the side of the road facing a law enforcement officer, or sit across from a government official claiming authority — and most of them have no idea that the authority being claimed has constitutional limits, that those limits are enforceable, and that the tools to enforce them are available to every citizen who knows they exist. Most do not know they exist. Jurisdiction is the threshold question that determines everything in any legal proceeding. What court has authority to decide this case. Over whom that authority extends. What law actually governs. Whether the constitutional rights the citizen carries into every proceeding are being honored or quietly set aside in favor of whatever the local ordinance happens to say. A court without jurisdiction has no authority to do anything. A judgment entered without jurisdiction is not a judgment. It is a legal nullity — void from the moment it was entered, challengeable at any time, in any proceeding, by any party against whom it is asserted. This book teaches every citizen how the system actually works. The American legal hierarchy places the Constitution at the top, federal law second, state law third, and municipal codes at the very bottom. That hierarchy is the explicit command of Article VI of the Constitution — the Supremacy Clause — and it binds every municipal court judge and every law enforcement officer regardless of what any local ordinance says. A constitutional right asserted against a municipal code is asserting supreme law against subordinate law. The Constitution wins. Every time. title: THE POWER OF SILENCE: How Estoppel, Conditional Acceptance, and the Unrebutted Affidavit T
description: Most Americans have never been taught the single most important thing the law has to say about silence: in specific circumstances, the legal system treats silence not as the absence of communication but as communication itself. When a creditor sends a demand and you do not respond, your silence can be treated as validation of the debt. When a government agency takes a position and you do not challenge it, your silence can make that position final. When a sworn statement of fact is served on a party who does not rebut it, those facts may stand as truth on the legal record. In law, silence is a choice — and the legal system assigns binding consequences to that choice whether you intended them or not. This book examines three interconnected legal doctrines that most Americans have never heard of but encounter the consequences of every day: estoppel, conditional acceptance, and the unrebutted affidavit. These are not fringe theories. They appear in Black’s Law Dictionary, in the Restatement Second of Contracts, in the Uniform Commercial Code, and in Supreme Court decisions stretching back more than a century. They are invoked in courtrooms every day by attorneys who understand them on behalf of clients who usually do not. Estoppel prevents a party from taking a position that contradicts what they previously said, did, or allowed to happen when another party relied on that prior conduct to their detriment. This book covers every recognized form: equitable estoppel, promissory estoppel, estoppel by silence and acquiescence, estoppel by record, estoppel by deed, administrative estoppel, and judicial estoppel. title: The Sovereign Citizen Trap : How the "No License to Practice Law" Myth Ends in Contempt, C
description: The Sovereign Citizen Trap: How the "No License to Practice Law" Myth Ends in Contempt, Criminal Charges, and Abandoned Clients is a forty-six-chapter treatise built around a single document: a courtroom filing template titled "Setup Template to Practice Law without a License, Represent Your Own Trusts and Corporations without a BAR Card," drafted in the first person and built to be filed. The document is not crude — it cites real cases and quotes them accurately — which is exactly what makes it dangerous. This book meets it on those terms, case by case. Part One shows what Dred Scott v. Sandford, the Slaughter House Cases, Bradwell v. Illinois, Yick Wo v. Hopkins, Ex parte Knowles, United States v. Anthony, and Van Valkenburg v. Brown actually held, and where the document's citation of each one breaks from that holding. Part Two dismantles the document's claim to a sole proprietorship exemption and its misreading of Corpus Juris Secundum. Part Three documents the real consequences of filing this argument: Rule 11 sanctions, contempt of court, and criminal prosecution for unauthorized practice of law, supported by a verified fifty state and D.C. enforcement survey. Part Four supplies the tools a judge, prosecutor, or opposing counsel needs in the moment — a recognition checklist, a model judicial order, a model motion to strike, bench notes, and referral procedures. Part Five collects the verified case excerpts, statute compendium, and table of authorities behind every claim. Later chapters extend the same method to material the document itself points readers toward: Meads v.
